content: The references provided include a comprehensive list of studies, guidelines, and expert contributions related to the management, diagnosis, and treatment of viral hemorrhagic fevers (VHFs) such as Ebola, Lassa fever, and Crimean-Congo hemorrhagic fever, as well as other related infectious diseases. These references highlight key clinical findings, laboratory features, and outcomes in patients affected by these diseases, as well as recommendations for case management, supportive care, and public health interventions. 1. Studies such as those by Erbay et al. (2008) and Hatipoglu et al. (2010) focus on the clinical and laboratory predictors of fatality in patients with Crimean-Congo hemorrhagic fever, providing insights into risk factors and outcomes in tertiary care settings. 2. Research by Kortepeter et al. (2011) and Schieffelin et al. (2014) examines the clinical features and outcomes of filoviral hemorrhagic fevers, including Ebola, with a focus on patient management in outbreak settings. 3. Dahmane et al. (2014) discuss the challenges in diagnosing and treating Lassa fever, particularly in rural hospitals, and the impact on mortality among children and women with obstetric conditions. 4. Blumberg et al. (2014) provide an overview of viral hemorrhagic fevers in the context of tropical diseases, emphasizing the importance of early diagnosis and management. 5. Studies on Lassa fever, such as those by McCormick et al. (1990) and Price et al. (1988), explore complications like acute sensorineural deafness and maternal-fetal outcomes during pregnancy. 6. WHO guidelines and interim recommendations address various aspects of managing VHFs, including infection prevention, nutritional care, and the use of personal protective equipment (PPE) during outbreaks. 7. Specific guidance is provided for managing Ebola virus disease in pregnancy, as detailed by Baggi et al. (2014) and Black et al. (2015), with a focus on maternal and neonatal outcomes. 8. Technical guidelines for integrated disease surveillance and response in the African region, as well as updates on managing severe acute malnutrition, are provided by WHO and UNICEF. 10. Contributions from experts and organizations, including the IMAI-IMCI Alliance, highlight collaborative efforts in developing and adapting clinical management tools for use in outbreak settings, supported by funding from international governments and agencies. These references collectively provide a robust foundation for understanding the clinical, epidemiological, and public health aspects of managing VHFs and related infectious diseases, with a focus on evidence-based practices and global health collaboration.
